practice_questions.text: Name the shot type in which a single facial feature, such as an eye or a mouth, fills the entire frame.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: extreme close-up.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'chiaroscuro' as it applies to film lighting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a lighting technique involving extreme contrast between light and dark areas of the image; 1 mark for explaining the effect (creates a sense of duality, mystery or moral ambiguity, often by lighting one side of a face while leaving the other in deep shadow). A purely dictionary definition without reference to film effect scores only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a low-angle shot of a villain in a confrontation sequence might affect the spectator's response. Refer to the specific framing choice and the meaning it generates.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying low-angle as a shot taken from below the subject; 1 mark for explaining that this makes the subject appear dominant or physically threatening; 1 mark for linking this to spectator response (e.g. the audience feels vulnerable, intimidated, or reminded of the antagonist's power); 1 mark for anchoring the explanation to a specific moment or sequence; 1 mark for precise use of specialist vocabulary (low angle, framing, spectator positioning, power dynamic).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how lighting choices in a scene of your choice from any film you have studied create atmosphere and position the spectator. Refer to at least two distinct lighting techniques in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Identifies at least two distinct, named lighting techniques (e.g. low-key, chiaroscuro, side-lighting, backlighting) anchored to a specific named sequence; clearly explains the effect of each technique on the spectator (e.g. creates unease, signals danger, constructs moral duality); links lighting choices to broader meaning (genre, character, theme); uses specialist vocabulary precisely and consistently throughout.

Secure (5-6): Identifies two techniques with mostly accurate description; generally explains spectator effect; one named sequence referenced; vocabulary mostly accurate.

Developing (3-4): Identifies one or two techniques but explanation of effect is generic (e.g. 'the lighting is dark and scary'); limited named sequences; vocabulary thin.

Emerging (1-2): Basic identification only; no explanation of effect on spectator; relies on plot description rather than analysis; vocabulary absent or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how cinematography shapes the spectator's experience of a moment of tension in a film you have studied. In your answer, refer to at least three distinct micro-features of cinematography (shot type, angle, movement or lighting) and explain the effect of each on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Three or more distinct micro-features identified with precision (specific shot type named, angle named, movement or lighting technique named); analysis stays tightly within one named sequence rather than spreading across the whole film; each feature is linked to a specific audience response; language is analytical rather than descriptive; specialist vocabulary is fluent.

Secure (7-8): Three micro-features addressed; mostly concrete and specific; generally accurate spectator responses stated; specialist vocabulary mostly correct.

Developing (4-6): One or two features addressed with limited specificity; some attempt at spectator effect but often vague ('the camera makes you feel scared'); may drift across more than one sequence rather than staying inside one short scene.

Emerging (1-3): Identifies a technique without analysing it; descriptive of plot rather than filmic choices; no named sequence; sparse or misused terminology.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how two films you have studied use camera angles to construct a character as powerful or powerless in one named sequence from each film. Refer to specific angle choices and their effect on the spectator.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (13-15): An explicit comparative line runs through every paragraph — moments are matched across the two films, differences are identified and explained in terms of context (e.g. genre, era, director's intent), and the answer ends in a synthesised contextual judgement about how angle choices serve each film's purposes differently; specialist vocabulary precise and consistent; at least one named sequence from each film.

Secure (9-12): Comparison is present throughout; two named sequences referenced; spectator effects stated; mostly accurate vocabulary; judgement present but may not be fully synthesised.

Developing (5-8): Some comparison attempted but may collapse into two separate single-film descriptions; sequences may not be named; spectator effect implied rather than stated.

Emerging (1-4): Two separate single-film descriptions with no comparative links; plot summary rather than analysis; vocabulary thin or absent.

before.exam_tip_html: When you use the command word “analyse” or “explain the effect”, the examiner wants to see a chain of reasoning, not just identification. The most common error on cinematography questions is naming a technique without explaining what it does to the spectator. A complete answer links three things: the specific technique (e.g. low-angle close-up), the named sequence it appears in (e.g. the opening chase), and the effect it creates for the audience (e.g. making the pursuer feel physically overwhelming and inescapable). For 8-mark and 10-mark questions, you must pick 2–3 distinct choices within a short sequence and unpack each one separately — do not describe the whole film. Think: technique → sequence → effect. That chain is the entire argument.

practice_questions.text: Name the court ruling that forced the major Hollywood studios to sell off their cinema chains in 1948.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Paramount decree (accept: United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc.; the 1948 antitrust ruling).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'vertical integration' as it applies to the classical Hollywood studio system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a single company owns more than one stage of the film supply chain; 1 mark for specifying at least two of the three stages: production, distribution and exhibition.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of the Hays Code on the narrative structure of studio-era genre films such as horror or the musical.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: identification of the Code as a self-regulatory censorship framework (1); explanation that it required moral transgression to be punished by the narrative close (1); application to a specific genre convention (e.g. the monster's destruction in horror, romantic coupling in the musical) (1); explanation that this shaped narrative cause-and-effect structures across the classical era (1); use of specialist vocabulary such as Production Code, narrative resolution, genre convention (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the shift from the studio contract system to the package-unit system changed the position of the director and the star within Hollywood film production. Refer to specific industrial changes in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: identifies both systems clearly; analyses the specific mechanisms of the change (loss of studio-guaranteed exhibition → rising risk → talent leverage); explains the consequence for the director (auteur creative control possible) and the star (brand financing power); uses precise specialist vocabulary (vertical integration, package-unit, distribution, exhibition, antitrust) throughout; demonstrates clear AO1 with AO2 application of institutional context to production outcomes.
Secure: both systems described with reasonable accuracy; at least one consequence for director or star analysed; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate; some AO2 application.
Developing: systems described but consequences mostly implicit; limited specialist vocabulary; answer reads more as description than analysis.
Emerging: basic recall of one system; little or no analysis of consequence; specialist vocabulary thin or absent.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how the industrial context of a film made during the classical studio era differs from one made during the blockbuster era, and explain how this context might shape the way a genre is handled differently in each film. Refer to one comparative pair from the unit in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: opens with a clear comparative line; matches a specific generic convention or narrative beat in both films; names the specific industrial difference (contract system vs package-unit; Hays Code vs ratings system; studio-guaranteed exhibition vs mass-release blockbuster logic); explains the contextual reason for the difference with precision; sustains specialist vocabulary (vertical integration, auteur, high-concept, production code, genre iconography) across every paragraph; ends with a synthesised contextual judgement rather than a summary of each film separately.
Secure: explicit comparative line in most paragraphs; at least two industrial differences named; one genre convention matched across both films; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate; some contextual judgement at the close.
Developing: relevant points about each film but comparative line is implicit or intermittent; industrial context noted rather than analysed; answer may read as two partial descriptions stitched together.
Emerging: one film described in reasonable detail, the other only briefly; no sustained comparative line; industrial context mentioned but not integrated into analysis; specialist vocabulary thin.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how understanding the industrial context of US mainstream cinema — from the studio system to the blockbuster era — helps a student analyse the differences between two films in a comparative pair. Reach a justified evaluative judgement about which contextual factor is most important for comparative analysis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: opens with a clear thesis identifying which contextual factor the student will argue is most important (e.g. the shift in production model, or the shift in regulatory context, or the shift in audience demographics); uses AO1 to establish the industrial facts accurately; weights AO2 by applying the facts to specific named moments or conventions in at least two films; integrates at least two distinct industrial factors (production model, regulatory context, commercial logic) and explains how each produces different filmic choices; uses specialist vocabulary (vertical integration, package-unit, auteur, high-concept, Paramount decree, Production Code) precisely throughout; ends with an evaluative judgement that is defended with evidence rather than merely asserted.
Secure: thesis present, if not always sustained; two industrial factors discussed; at least one specific film reference used to support an analytical claim; AO2 present but may not consistently outweigh AO1; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: relevant knowledge of the industrial context; analysis present but may default to description of the periods rather than application to films; specialist vocabulary used but sometimes imprecisely; limited evaluative judgement.
Emerging: basic recall of one or two industrial facts; little analysis of how context shapes film; no clear thesis; specialist vocabulary thin or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: In which year did the Lumiere brothers hold their first public film screening?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 1895.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'montage' in the context of Soviet cinema?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that montage is an editing technique; 1 mark for explaining that it involves juxtaposing contrasting shots so that their collision creates a new idea or emotion not present in either image alone (Eisenstein's approach).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect that the introduction of synchronised sound had on camera movement in films made in the late 1920s and early 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that cameras became less mobile; 1 mark for explaining that cameras had to be enclosed in heavy sound-proof blimps to prevent mechanical noise appearing on the soundtrack; 1 mark for explaining that microphones had to be hidden on set, restricting actor and camera movement; 1 mark for linking this to a consequence for visual storytelling (films became more static, losing the kinetic camerawork developed in the late silent era); 1 mark for use of accurate specialist vocabulary (e.g. Vitaphone, synchronised sound, continuity editing, tracking shot).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of Eisenstein's montage technique differed from Hollywood's approach to continuity editing. In your answer, explain what each technique does and what effect it creates for the spectator.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise account of both techniques, with a clear explanation of the difference in editorial philosophy. Continuity editing is identified as aiming to make cuts invisible, preserving coherent time and space and guiding the spectator smoothly through narrative. Montage is explained as a deliberate collision of contrasting images designed to produce an idea or emotion beyond either shot. The spectator's experience of each is specifically addressed: continuity editing creates immersion and identifies with characters; montage creates an intellectual and emotional impact through juxtaposition. Appropriate examples are used (e.g. Griffith's cross-cutting, Eisenstein's image-collision sequences). Specialist vocabulary is precise and sustained throughout.
Secure: Both techniques are explained and the key difference is identified. At least one effect on the spectator is stated. Some specialist vocabulary is used.
Developing: One technique is explained more fully than the other, or the difference is recognised without the spectator-effect being articulated. Vocabulary is present but may be imprecise.
Emerging: Basic description of one technique only, with little or no explanation of effect. Descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Identify the name of the sound system used in The Jazz Singer (1927) and state which studio produced the film.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Vitaphone (sound system) and Warner Bros. (studio). Both required for the mark; accept either alone for half credit if the mark scheme allows partial credit.

practice_questions.text: Explain what three-strip Technicolor was and why its use was restricted mainly to prestige productions and musicals in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that three-strip Technicolor used three separate strips of film recording red, green and blue light simultaneously; 1 mark for explaining that it produced rich, saturated colour not achievable by earlier processes; 1 mark for identifying that the specialist camera was rented (not sold) by the Technicolor Corporation; 1 mark for explaining that the process was expensive and slow, and required Technicolor's own colour consultants on set; 1 mark for linking these institutional constraints to the consequence that only large-scale studios could afford it for high-budget productions.

practice_questions.text: Identify one film festival that has been a key launchpad for American independent cinema since the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Sundance Film Festival (accept: Sundance). Other credible answers (Toronto International Film Festival, SXSW) accepted with appropriate justification, but Sundance is the expected answer given the lesson content.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'specialty division' in the context of American film distribution?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is a distribution arm or subsidiary of a major Hollywood studio; 1 mark for explaining that it handles smaller, more distinctive or niche films that the main studio label would not typically release. Example: Fox Searchlight as the specialty division of 20th Century Fox.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the foundation of the Sundance Film Festival changed the conditions for American independent filmmakers. Refer to at least one specific effect on production or distribution.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for accurately identifying Sundance as a festival launchpad (founded 1978, relaunched mid-1980s); 1 mark for explaining its role in giving independent films visibility; 1 mark for explaining the effect on distribution (e.g. studios and specialty divisions attending to acquire films); 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. Tarantino, Soderbergh, or the Whiplash short-to-feature route); 1 mark for a developed point about how the festival model shaped audience access to indie film.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the industrial conditions of American independent cinema shape a director's filmic choices. Refer to at least two specific examples of how budget or creative autonomy affects the finished film.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly distinguishes between independent and specialty-division models; analyses at least two specific filmic choices (e.g. naturalistic performance, long static takes, location shooting) and directly links each to an industrial condition (limited budget, absence of final-cut demands, small crew); uses specialist vocabulary (auteur, mumblecore, production context, distribution model); demonstrates understanding that aesthetic choices are often consequences of industrial ones.

Secure: Identifies at least two industrial conditions and links each to a filmic outcome; uses mostly accurate vocabulary; may be less precise about which companies are specialty divisions and which are genuinely independent.

Developing: Identifies indie film as different from mainstream Hollywood but explains the difference only in stylistic terms (handheld, low budget) without connecting these to specific industrial conditions; vocabulary generally accurate but limited.

Emerging: Describes indie films as small or different without explaining the industrial category; no specific examples of filmic choices linked to production context; little or no specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the changing landscape of American independent film distribution from the 1990s to the 2020s reflects shifting relationships between artistic independence and commercial success. Refer to at least two named organisations or filmmakers in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces the shift from Miramax/Disney (1993 acquisition) through the late-2000s specialty-division peak (Fox Searchlight, Focus Features) to the A24 model; names specific films or directors at each stage; analyses the tension between commercial viability and artistic autonomy as an ongoing structural problem rather than a simple decline narrative; uses specialist vocabulary consistently (auteur, specialty division, distribution model, festival circuit).

Secure: Covers at least two named organisations with reasonably accurate dates; identifies the core tension between independence and commercial pressure; vocabulary mostly accurate; may not fully develop the argument about how the industrial conditions shift.

Developing: Aware that Miramax and A24 are different kinds of companies but struggles to explain how or why; limited named evidence; discussion stays largely descriptive rather than analytical.

Emerging: Basic identification of indie film as separate from Hollywood; minimal named evidence; no real analytical engagement with the industrial categories.

practice_questions.text: As a critic of American independent cinema, evaluate how accurately the term 'independent' describes the films produced within the specialty-division studio model. Reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Opens with a clear thesis (e.g. the term 'independent' is now more industrial myth than reality for most commercially successful US indie films, though genuine independence persists at the micro-budget level); sustains the argument across multiple paragraphs; uses at least two named companies or films as concrete evidence; weighs the tension between artistic autonomy and commercial ownership with nuance; integrates relevant critical or contextual framing (e.g. auteurism, the festival circuit as a market); closes with a justified evaluative judgement that acknowledges complexity; specialist vocabulary used precisely throughout.

Secure: Has a thesis; covers at least two relevant named cases; engages with the tension between independence and commercial backing; vocabulary mostly accurate; judgement present but may be underargued.

Developing: Describes the difference between indie and mainstream but does not sustain an argument; evidence limited to one named example; vocabulary used but sometimes imprecisely; no clear evaluative judgement.

Emerging: Identifies indie as different from Hollywood in general terms; minimal named evidence; no thesis; no evaluative judgement; vocabulary thin or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: Identify the director of Jojo Rabbit (2019).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Taika Waititi.

practice_questions.text: What is a frame narrative? Use the term correctly in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a frame narrative is a story embedded within another (outer) story; 1 mark for using correct specialist register (e.g. outer narrative / present-tense frame / inner story / retrospective).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the mockumentary opening of District 9 positions the spectator differently from a conventional fictional opening. Refer to specific camera or editing choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying the mockumentary technique (news footage, talking-head interviews, handheld 16mm); 1 mark for naming a specific camera or editing choice (e.g. handheld instability, news-ticker framing, intercutting archive and interview footage); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the spectator (e.g. positions spectator as an informed observer with apparent institutional authority, or creates a sense of documentary realism); 1 mark for linking to the narrative break-point when the film shifts to conventional fiction (e.g. the shift signals loss of institutional control); 1 mark for accurate use of specialist vocabulary (mockumentary, diegesis, narrative register, spectator positioning).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the cross-cutting structure of the opening interrogation sequence in Slumdog Millionaire shapes the spectator's relationship to narrative information. Refer to at least two specific editing or cinematographic choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Answer analyses at least two specific editing or cinematographic choices within the named sequence (e.g. cross-cutting between police station, quiz-show studio and childhood flashback; handheld camera in the interrogation; saturated colour shift between time periods) and links each choice to a precise effect on the spectator's knowledge or emotional position (e.g. the cross-cut places the spectator as a retrospective investigator; the colour saturation signals memory). Macro meaning is stated (frame narrative as machinery of suspense and revelation; narrative withholding as a source of dramatic irony). Specialist vocabulary is precise throughout.

Secure: Two choices identified with generally accurate effect on spectator; named sequence clearly referenced; some macro link to narrative structure; mostly accurate vocabulary.

Developing: One choice identified; effect on spectator implied but not stated; may drift toward plot summary; limited vocabulary.

Emerging: Generic description of the sequence without specific editing or cinematographic choices; no analysis of spectator positioning; vocabulary thin or absent.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how Nora Twomey uses the embedded narrative structure in The Breadwinner to create meaning. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained thesis is present from the outset and maintained (e.g. arguing that the embedded storybook sequences create a dramatic irony that reframes the outer narrative’s danger as survivable). At least two named sequences are analysed with concrete micro-features (e.g. the storybook frame-tale insets: the shift in animation style — more abstract and stylised — signals entry into the inner story; voice-over and rhythm of narration position the spectator as the listener as well as observer). Macro meaning is sustained (embedded narrative as a coping mechanism; the inner story’s symbolic monsters commenting on the outer world). A named theory or framework is integrated appropriately (e.g. Bordwell on information organisation; the dramatic irony of the spectator knowing more than the protagonist can articulate). Specialist vocabulary used precisely throughout. Evaluative judgement is justified with reference to evidence from the film.

Secure: Thesis present; two sequences referenced; micro-features identified but analysis of effect may be partial; macro meaning present; some specialist vocabulary; judgement reached.

Developing: Some relevant points; limited reference to named sequences; analysis may collapse into description; limited specialist vocabulary; weak or absent judgement.

Emerging: Plot summary dominates; no thesis; no named sequences used analytically; minimal specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Taika Waititi uses a child's-eye-view narrative in Jojo Rabbit to withhold information from the spectator. Refer to the imaginary-Hitler dance opening sequence.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying the child’s-eye-view narration device; 1 mark for naming a specific choice in the opening sequence (e.g. symmetrical framing, anachronistic David Bowie music, the imaginary companion as a distorted fantasy projection); 1 mark for explaining how this withholds real-world information (the spectator sees Nazi Germany through the distorting lens of a child’s fantasy, so political horror is initially displaced); 1 mark for explaining the effect on spectator positioning (we are positioned inside Jojo’s consciousness rather than given an objective view); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (unreliable narration, spectator positioning, mise-en-scene, child’s-eye-view, satirical register).

practice_questions.text: Who invented the Steadicam?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Garrett Brown.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'CinemaScope'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that CinemaScope is a widescreen film process introduced in 1953 (by 20th Century Fox); 1 mark for explaining that it used an anamorphic lens to squeeze a wide image onto standard 35mm film, producing an aspect ratio of approximately 2.55:1.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect that the Paramount decree of 1948 had on the Hollywood studio system and on the kinds of films studios made in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the Paramount decree forced studios to sell their cinema chains (end of vertical integration); 1 mark for explaining that without guaranteed screen access studios could no longer be certain of a return on every film made; 1 mark for identifying television as a concurrent threat driving down cinema attendance; 1 mark for explaining that studios responded with spectacular technologies (widescreen, 3D, colour) to offer audiences something television could not; 1 mark for linking this to a specific example (e.g. CinemaScope introduced by 20th Century Fox in 1953) or for accurate use of terminology (vertical integration, aspect ratio, spectacle).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of the Steadicam changed what directors could achieve with camera movement. Refer to at least one specific film example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise account of what the Steadicam does (body-mounted stabilisation system isolating the camera from the operator's body movement) and what it enabled (smooth continuous tracking through complex spaces without rails or dolly). The answer articulates the specific difference from both pure handheld (jerky, urgent, human-feeling) and pure dolly work (smooth but constrained to flat surfaces and pre-laid tracks). At least one named film example is analysed: the most credit-worthy is Kubrick's The Shining (1980), where the Steadicam tracking a child on a tricycle along hotel corridors produced a psychological sensation of something inhuman, patient and predatory. The link between the micro-choice (Steadicam) and the macro-meaning (dread, threat) is explicit. Specialist vocabulary is accurate and sustained.
Secure: The Steadicam is correctly explained and the key advantage is identified. At least one film example is named with some analysis of effect. Vocabulary is mostly accurate.
Developing: The Steadicam is described but the specific difference from other camera movement types is unclear. Film example named but effect on spectator is implied rather than stated.
Emerging: Basic description of what a Steadicam is, with no or very generic film example. No analysis of macro-level effect.

practice_questions.text: What was the name of the company George Lucas founded in 1975 to produce visual effects?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Industrial Light and Magic (ILM). Accept: ILM.

practice_questions.text: Explain how early CGI in films such as Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) and Jurassic Park (1993) changed what filmmakers could put on screen. In your answer, refer to specific examples of what these films achieved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that CGI allowed filmmakers to create characters, environments or effects that could not be filmed practically; 1 mark for a specific example from Terminator 2 (the T-1000 reforming from a liquid-metal pool, demonstrating convincing organic movement); 1 mark for a specific example from Jurassic Park (dinosaurs composited into wide live-action shots, casting shadows on real ground); 1 mark for explaining compositing as the digital process of combining generated elements with live-action footage so they appear to share the same physical space; 1 mark for explaining the consequence for audiences or storytelling (seamless integration meant audiences accepted the impossible as real, expanding the range of narrative and visual experiences cinema could offer).

practice_questions.text: Name the cinematographer of Dracula (1931) and state the European film tradition his lighting style drew on.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Karl Freund, drawing on Weimar German expressionism (accept: German expressionism; expressionist cinema).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'non-diegetic sound' and give one example of its use in The Lost Boys (1987).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a definition that captures sound not originating within the story world, heard only by the audience; 1 mark for a relevant example from The Lost Boys such as the rock soundtrack playing over the boardwalk-arrival sequence or the gang initiation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the mise-en-scene of the opening at Castle Dracula positions the spectator in relation to the vampire.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: identification of a specific element of mise-en-scene in the castle opening (1); description of a concrete visual detail — e.g. the low-key lighting, the diagonal staircase composition, the theatrical blocking (1); explanation of the spectator effect — e.g. unease, awe, the sense of the monster as architectural presence (1); connection of the micro choice to the macro meaning of the vampire as static foreign threat (1); use of specialist vocabulary such as mise-en-scene, expressionism, composition, spectator positioning (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the editing of the cliff-hang gang initiation sequence in The Lost Boys constructs vampirism as aspiration rather than threat. Refer to at least two distinct editing choices in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: stays within the named sequence; identifies at least two distinct editing choices (e.g. accelerating cut rate, cuts on the music beat, match cuts on movement) and analyses the effect of each on the spectator; links editing to sound design and the music-video aesthetic; makes the macro meaning explicit — vampirism glamorised, transgression as freedom; uses specialist vocabulary (cut rate, non-diegetic, continuity, juxtaposition, music-video editing) precisely throughout.
Secure: two editing choices identified; effect on spectator stated for at least one; some macro connection to the idea of vampirism as aspiration; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: one editing choice identified with some explanation; macro meaning implied but not stated; answer may describe the sequence generally rather than staying inside specific editing choices.
Emerging: some description of the sequence; editing mentioned but not analysed; macro meaning absent; specialist vocabulary thin.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how cinematography and sound are used to construct the moment when a human character first encounters the vampire in Dracula (1931) and The Lost Boys (1987). Match one moment from each film and explain the contextual reason for the difference.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: opens with a clear comparative claim; matches a comparable first-encounter moment in each film (e.g. the eye-light close-up meeting with Mina vs the boardwalk-arrival first sight of the gang); identifies specific cinematography and sound differences (expressionist low-key lighting and near-silence vs saturated neon and non-diegetic rock); explains the spectator effect for each; provides the contextual reason — 1931 studio era / Production Code / expressionist tradition vs 1987 blockbuster / MTV aesthetic / teen commercial market; sustains specialist vocabulary throughout; ends with a synthesised comparative judgement.
Secure: explicit comparative line in most paragraphs; both micro-elements addressed; contextual reason given; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: relevant points but comparison may be implicit; only one micro-element sustained; contextual reason noted rather than analysed.
Emerging: one film analysed in more depth than the other; little or no explicit comparative line; contextual reason absent.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the vampire figure in Dracula (1931) and The Lost Boys (1987) functions as a carrier of the social anxieties of its respective era. In your answer, refer to specific named sequences from both films and analyse the filmic choices that construct the monster’s meaning. Reach a justified evaluative judgement about which film more effectively uses the vampire as social metaphor.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: opens with a clear thesis identifying the social-anxiety argument and stating which film the student will argue makes more effective use of the metaphor; uses AO1 to establish the production contexts briefly and accurately (1931 Depression-era Universal, 1987 Reaganite consumer culture); weights AO2 by applying the contextual knowledge to specific named sequences (castle opening and eye-light close-up for Dracula; boardwalk arrival and cliff-hang initiation for The Lost Boys); analyses at least three specific micro-choices from named sequences across both films; integrates a film theory or analytical concept with precision — e.g. the monster as displaced social anxiety (genre theory), the gaze (Mulvey) applied to the eye-light close-up; uses specialist vocabulary (mise-en-scene, expressionism, iconography, non-diegetic, gaze, genre convention, spectator positioning) precisely throughout; ends with a defended evaluative judgement.
Secure: thesis present; both films discussed with reference to at least two named sequences; AO2 present but may not consistently outweigh AO1; two micro-choices analysed; contextual link to social anxiety in each era made; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: relevant knowledge of both films; some analysis but may default to description; named sequences mentioned but not closely unpacked; one era’s social anxiety discussed more fully than the other; limited evaluative judgement.
Emerging: basic description of both films; social-anxiety idea acknowledged but not developed; no sustained micro-analysis of named sequences; specialist vocabulary thin or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: Identify one element of mise-en-scene other than the set or setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: costume/wardrobe; props; make-up; performance/blocking/actor positioning. Setting/set alone scores 0 as the question explicitly excludes it.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'mise-en-scene' in film analysis?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is a French term meaning 'placing on stage' (or 'placing in the scene/frame'); 1 mark for demonstrating that it encompasses all visual elements placed before the camera including setting, costume, props, make-up and performance (not just set design). A definition that limits mise-en-scene to only set or lighting scores no more than 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of a signature prop in one sequence of a film you have studied creates meaning for the spectator. Refer to the specific object, the sequence it appears in, and the effect it has.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for naming a specific prop from a named sequence; 1 mark for describing its literal function in the narrative; 1 mark for explaining its symbolic or character-signifying dimension; 1 mark for linking this to spectator response (what the audience understands or feels because of the prop); 1 mark for precise use of specialist vocabulary (signature prop, visual motif, mise-en-scene, symbolic, spectator positioning).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how costume choices in a specific sequence of a film you have studied communicate character or theme to the spectator. Refer to at least two distinct costume or wardrobe details.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Two or more named, precise costume details from a named sequence (e.g. colour, fabric, fit, condition); each detail linked to a specific meaning (character status, psychological state, social context, thematic idea); spectator effect clearly stated for each; specialist vocabulary (colour palette, character signifier, mise-en-scene, wardrobe, visual motif) used precisely.

Secure (5-6): Two details addressed; meaning generally stated; spectator effect present but may be imprecise; mostly correct vocabulary.

Developing (3-4): One detail described with some attempt at meaning; effect on spectator implied rather than stated; vocabulary limited.

Emerging (1-2): Describes what a character is wearing without explaining what it means; relies on plot summary rather than analysis of visual choices.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how mise-en-scene elements in one short sequence of a film you have studied work together to construct a sense of place and character. In your answer, refer to at least three distinct elements of mise-en-scene and explain the spectator effect of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Three distinct elements of mise-en-scene (from setting, costume, props, make-up, blocking) named precisely and with specific visual detail; analysis stays within one named short sequence; each element linked to a spectator effect and to a broader meaning (theme, character, genre); specialist vocabulary is fluent; description is spatial and precise rather than vague.

Secure (7-8): Three elements addressed; at least two with specific visual detail; spectator effects mostly stated; one named sequence; vocabulary mostly accurate.

Developing (4-6): One or two elements with limited visual specificity; effect on spectator implied; may drift beyond one sequence; vocabulary thin.

Emerging (1-3): Lists mise-en-scene elements without describing or analysing them; mostly plot summary; no named sequence; vocabulary absent or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how mise-en-scene is used in two films you have studied to communicate the social status or power of a central character. Refer to one named sequence from each film and at least two elements of mise-en-scene in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (13-15): Explicit comparative line through every paragraph — matched moments from both films, differences in approach identified and explained by context (genre, era, cultural setting); at least two named sequences; social or power meanings precisely stated; ends in a synthesised contextual judgement about how each film uses mise-en-scene for different ends; specialist vocabulary fluent.

Secure (9-12): Comparison present throughout; two named sequences; social/power meanings addressed; vocabulary mostly correct; some synthesis in conclusion.

Developing (5-8): Two films addressed but comparison may collapse into sequential single-film descriptions; sequences may not be named; social meaning may be implied rather than argued.

Emerging (1-4): Two separate single-film summaries with no comparative links; mainly plot description; specialist vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: Who wrote the screenplay for Juno (2007)?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Diablo Cody.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'non-diegetic sound' in film analysis?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that non-diegetic sound originates from outside the world of the story; 1 mark for an example or further clarification (e.g. a musical score or a narrator's voice that the characters cannot hear).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the choice of non-diegetic music in the opening convenience-store sequence of Juno positions the spectator emotionally before the narrative's central situation is fully established.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying Barry Louis Polisar’s ‘All I Want Is You’ as the opening non-diegetic song; 1 mark for describing the quality of the sound (lo-fi, acoustic, fragile); 1 mark for explaining the effect on tone (signals warmth and lightness before the pregnancy reveal); 1 mark for connecting this to a macro effect on the spectator (pre-empts potential melodrama, establishes the film's register as tonal comedy); 1 mark for a developed point about how this is a directorial choice that reflects an authorial decision about genre.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how mise-en-scene in the Loring living-room first-meeting sequence constructs meaning about the characters and their relationships. Refer to at least three specific elements within the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Stays inside the named sequence; analyses at least three distinct elements of mise-en-scene (e.g. set design/colour palette, costume, spatial blocking/positioning); for each element states what it signifies about character or theme (e.g. Vanessa's palette-matching costume signals belonging; Mark's spatial marginalisation signals alienation); links micro observations to macro meanings (the power dynamic within the Loring marriage, the film's non-judgemental stance); uses specialist vocabulary precisely throughout (mise-en-scene, blocking, two-shot, over-shoulder, palette).

Secure: Identifies at least two elements of mise-en-scene with mostly accurate analysis; connects at least one element to character or theme; vocabulary generally accurate; may not sustain the analysis across the whole sequence.

Developing: Describes what is visible (the room is neat, Mark wears a band T-shirt) without fully explaining what these choices signify; vocabulary limited; effect on spectator implied rather than stated.

Emerging: General description of the scene; no use of the term mise-en-scene; no specific elements identified; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Jason Reitman uses cinematography and mise-en-scene in the Loring living-room first-meeting sequence of Juno to construct character relationships without relying on dialogue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Stays inside the named sequence; analyses cinematography (static medium two-shots, over-shoulder exchanges, absence of editorial close-ups) and mise-en-scene (set palette, Vanessa's costume matching the room, Mark's spatial marginalisation) as a linked system; states the effect on the spectator for each choice (the camera's observational restraint positions the audience as non-judgemental witnesses); links micro choices to macro meaning (the Loring marriage's power dynamics, the film's broader non-judgemental stance); specialist vocabulary precise throughout.

Secure: Identifies at least two elements across cinematography and mise-en-scene; connects at least one to character meaning; generally accurate vocabulary; effect on spectator mostly stated.

Developing: Describes what is visible (the room is tidy, there are close-ups and wide shots) without fully explaining what these choices create; vocabulary limited; stays largely descriptive.

Emerging: General description of the scene; no named micro-features; no analysis of effect; specialist vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how Jason Reitman uses the indie-folk soundtrack in Juno to develop character and establish tone. Refer to at least two named sequences in your answer and use specialist film vocabulary throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Opens with a thesis about the function of the soundtrack as characterisation and tone-setting device, not mere decoration; analyses at least two named sequences (e.g. the opening convenience-store sequence, the closing porch duet); for each sequence analyses the specific relationship between diegetic and non-diegetic sound with appropriate terminology (needle-drop, sound bridge, non-diegetic score); connects micro sound-design choices to macro meanings (tonal comedy, Juno's characterisation as emotionally vulnerable beneath the wit, the film's non-judgemental stance); integrates relevant production context (Fox Searchlight distribution, Cody's screenplay as authorial voice, the lo-fi aesthetic as indie signifier); sustains specialist vocabulary; closes with a justified evaluative judgement about how successfully the soundtrack achieves its dual function.

Secure: Has a thesis; covers at least two sequences; makes accurate use of diegetic/non-diegetic distinction; connects at least one sound choice to character or tone; vocabulary mostly accurate; judgement present but may be underargued.

Developing: Aware that the soundtrack is important but analysis stays at the level of 'the music is cheerful' or 'the music fits the mood'; minimal use of technical vocabulary; evidence limited to one sequence; no sustained thesis.

Emerging: Identifies music as present in the film; no technical analysis; no named sequences; no thesis; plot description rather than analysis.

practice_questions.text: Which film, released in 1995, was the world's first feature-length computer-generated animated film?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Toy Story.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'streaming' in relation to film distribution?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that streaming is a method of delivering film content over the internet directly to the viewer's device; 1 mark for explaining that it requires no physical media (such as DVD or Blu-ray) and no downloading of files — content is accessed and played in real time.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect that digital cinematography had on the economics of film production, and how this contributed to the democratisation of filmmaking.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that digital cinematography removed the per-take cost of film stock (no expensive celluloid to buy or process); 1 mark for explaining that footage could be reviewed immediately on set, encouraging more experimentation; 1 mark for identifying that consumer-grade digital and smartphone cameras made equipment affordable outside the studio system; 1 mark for linking this to the democratisation of production (filmmakers from communities previously excluded by cost barriers could now make feature films); 1 mark for a named example such as Tangerine (2015, Sean Baker, iPhone 5S) or for accurate use of terminology.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of smartphone filmmaking, as demonstrated by Tangerine (2015), changed what kinds of stories cinema could tell and whose stories were told.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer explains what Tangerine demonstrated technically (shot entirely on iPhone 5S with anamorphic lens adaptor; Filmic Pro app) and articulates how the technology shaped the aesthetic (close framing, immediacy, soft-focus backgrounds). The answer then makes the macro-level argument: the low cost and mobility of smartphone cameras enabled directors without studio budgets to make work about communities and stories that the traditional studio system's financial logic had excluded. Tangerine's subject matter (transgender sex workers in Los Angeles) is identified as an example of a story that found a form of production suited to its scale and community. The link between technology (micro: specific camera choice, specific visual properties) and institutional/representational consequence (macro: democratisation, diversification of whose stories are told) is explicit and sustained. Specialist vocabulary is precise throughout.
Secure: The technological facts are correct and the main point about democratisation is made. Some link between the specific camera and its aesthetic effect is present. Subject matter of Tangerine is referenced.
Developing: The film is correctly identified as shot on an iPhone but analysis of the aesthetic or representational consequence is thin. Vocabulary is present but imprecise.
Emerging: Basic correct identification of the film with little or no analysis of effect on storytelling or representation.

practice_questions.text: In what year did Netflix launch its online streaming service?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 2007.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Avengers: Infinity War (2018) is historically significant in relation to IMAX technology, and what effect this had on the audience's cinema experience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Avengers: Infinity War (2018, directed by Anthony and Joe Russo) was the first major fiction feature shot entirely on IMAX cameras; 1 mark for distinguishing this from films merely shown in IMAX (upscaled presentation vs capture format); 1 mark for explaining that IMAX cameras produce images significantly larger and sharper than standard 35mm; 1 mark for explaining the effect on audience experience (the image quality could fill a six-storey screen with detail visible from the back, creating a theatrical spectacle qualitatively different from home viewing); 1 mark for relating this to the broader context (studios competing with streaming platforms by offering a premium theatrical experience that cannot be replicated at home).

practice_questions.text: Name the type of edit that switches instantaneously between two shots with no transitional effect.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a cut (also accept: straight cut, hard cut).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'continuity editing'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that continuity editing is a system of assembling shots to create the illusion of continuous time and space; 1 mark for naming at least one specific convention it relies on (e.g. the 180-degree rule, eye-line match, shot-reverse-shot). A definition that only says 'editing that flows smoothly' without naming a convention or principle scores 1 mark at most.

practice_questions.text: Explain how cross-cutting in an action or chase sequence of a film you have studied creates tension for the spectator. Refer to the specific editing choices and their effect.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying cross-cutting as alternating between two or more simultaneous strands of action; 1 mark for naming a specific sequence from a studied film where cross-cutting occurs; 1 mark for explaining how the juxtaposition of the two strands creates tension (the spectator knows both events are happening simultaneously and wonders whether they will converge); 1 mark for noting how pace (accelerating cut rate) intensifies this effect; 1 mark for precise specialist vocabulary (cross-cutting, parallel editing, juxtaposition, pace, spectator response).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how editing pace in one named sequence of a film you have studied shapes the spectator's emotional response. Refer to at least two specific editing choices (such as cut length, rhythm, or the use of a specific transition type).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Two or more named editing choices (e.g. accelerating cut rate, long take, jump cut, dissolve) from a named sequence; each choice precisely described in terms of duration and effect; spectator response stated for each (e.g. accelerating pace generates urgency; a sudden long take forces unwanted proximity); links to macro meaning (narrative tension, character interiority, genre expectations); specialist vocabulary precise and consistent.

Secure (5-6): Two editing choices addressed; named sequence referenced; spectator effect generally stated; vocabulary mostly correct.

Developing (3-4): One editing choice described with some spectator effect; may be vague ('the editing is fast and exciting'); limited named sequence reference.

Emerging (1-2): Identifies that there is fast or slow editing without explaining effect; relies on plot description; no named sequence; vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how editing within one short sequence of a film you have studied constructs narrative tension. Stay within the sequence and refer to at least three distinct editing micro-features: the type of cuts used, the pace and rhythm of editing, and any specific transition techniques.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Three distinct editing micro-features identified with precision within a single named sequence; each feature described concretely (e.g. 'cuts of approximately one second each, shortening to under half a second as the sequence reaches its climax'); spectator effect clearly stated for each; analysis stays inside the sequence rather than surveying the whole film; specialist vocabulary fluent throughout.

Secure (7-8): Three micro-features addressed; analysis mostly stays within one sequence; spectator effects stated; vocabulary mostly accurate.

Developing (4-6): One or two features; may spread across the whole film rather than staying inside a sequence; effect on spectator implied rather than stated.

Emerging (1-3): Lists editing terms without analysing their effect; mainly plot description; no named sequence; vocabulary thin or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how editing is used in two films you have studied to construct a moment of high tension or danger. Refer to one named sequence from each film and at least two editing techniques in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (13-15): Explicit comparative line through every paragraph — two named sequences, matched moment by moment across the two films, with differences in editing approach identified and linked to contextual reasons (genre, era, director's aesthetic, film's tone); ends in a synthesised judgement about how each film uses editing for its own specific purposes; at least two editing techniques per film; specialist vocabulary precise.

Secure (9-12): Comparison present; two named sequences; editing techniques named; spectator effects addressed; vocabulary mostly accurate; some synthesis.

Developing (5-8): Some comparison attempted but may collapse into sequential single-film descriptions; may not name sequences precisely; spectator effect implied.

Emerging (1-4): Two separate single-film descriptions stitched together with no comparative links; mainly plot summary; vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: Name the producer of the MGM unit responsible for Singin' in the Rain (1952).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Arthur Freed (accept: the Freed Unit).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'integrated musical' and explain how it differs from a musical in which numbers are staged as interruptions to the narrative.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a definition capturing that songs and dance arise organically from narrative situation and character motivation; 1 mark for contrasting this with a model where numbers stop the narrative rather than extending it.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the choice of a locked-off master shot for the title number in Singin' in the Rain shapes the spectator's understanding of the performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: identification of the locked-off master shot (1); description of how it keeps the dancer's whole body in frame (1); explanation that this honours the physical craft of the performance rather than implying it requires editing assistance (1); connection to the film's broader self-reflexive theme about authentic performance (1); use of specialist vocabulary such as master shot, continuity editing, self-reflexivity, mise-en-scene (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how editing and cinematography in the 'Greased Lightnin'' garage number construct musical spectacle as a commercial event rather than as a display of individual performance. Refer to at least three specific micro-choices in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: stays within the named sequence; identifies at least three distinct micro-choices (e.g. rapid cut rate, crane shot, panning shot, saturated colour palette, 1970s studio-sound performance); analyses the effect of each on the spectator; makes the macro meaning explicit — spectacle as commercial event, energy over legibility; connects to the film’s industrial context (blockbuster era, chart album tie-in); uses specialist vocabulary (continuity editing, mise-en-scene, non-diegetic, montage, cinematography) precisely.
Secure: three micro-choices identified; effect on spectator stated for at least two; some macro connection to commercial spectacle; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: two micro-choices identified; macro meaning implied; answer may describe the sequence generally rather than unpacking specific choices.
Emerging: some description of the sequence; one micro-choice mentioned; macro meaning absent; specialist vocabulary thin.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how the solo ballad number in Singin' in the Rain and in Grease uses camera movement and sound design to construct the emotional interiority of the performing character. Match one named number from each film.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: opens with a clear comparative claim; matches a named solo ballad from each film (e.g. the title number or ‘Good Morning’ vs Sandy’s ‘Hopelessly Devoted to You’, or the slow-push-in mechanics of solo staging in both); identifies specific camera movement differences (locked-off vs slow push-in) and sound design differences (diegetic vocal performance integrated with non-diegetic orchestration vs clearly non-diegetic studio recording); explains the spectator effect for each; provides the contextual reason — Freed Unit investment in performer authenticity vs late-1970s commercial ballad convention; sustains specialist vocabulary throughout; ends with a synthesised comparative judgement.
Secure: explicit comparative line in most paragraphs; camera movement and sound addressed; contextual reason given; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: relevant points but comparison implicit; only one element sustained; contextual reason noted but not developed.
Emerging: one film analysed more fully than the other; no sustained comparative line; contextual reason absent.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how Singin' in the Rain (1952) and Grease (1978) each use the Hollywood musical form to construct a particular relationship between nostalgia, performance and spectacle. In your answer, refer to specific named sequences from both films and analyse the filmic choices that shape the spectator's experience. Reach a justified evaluative judgement about which film makes more self-aware use of the musical as a form.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: opens with a clear thesis stating a position on which film uses the musical form more self-awarely; uses AO1 to establish the production contexts briefly and accurately (MGM Freed Unit 1952 vs Paramount blockbuster 1978); weights AO2 by applying the contextual knowledge to specific named sequences (title number and ‘Make ‘Em Laugh’ for Singin’ in the Rain; garage number and closing transformation for Grease); analyses at least three specific micro-choices from named sequences across both films; integrates a film theory or analytical concept — e.g. the integrated musical as a generic mode, self-reflexivity as a formal strategy, nostalgia as ideological packaging; uses specialist vocabulary (integrated musical, Technicolor, continuity editing, non-diegetic, self-reflexivity, auteur, spectacle, genre convention) precisely throughout; ends with a defended evaluative judgement.
Secure: thesis present; both films discussed with reference to at least two named sequences; AO2 present but may not consistently outweigh AO1; two micro-choices analysed; some comparative line sustained.
Developing: relevant knowledge of both films; analysis present but may default to description; named sequences referenced but not closely unpacked; evaluative judgement limited.
Emerging: basic description of both films; nostalgia or performance idea acknowledged but not developed; no sustained micro-analysis; specialist vocabulary thin.

practice_questions.text: Identify the country of production for Wadjda (2012).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Saudi Arabia (accept Saudi Arabia / Germany co-production).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'counter-type' in the context of film representation? Give an example from one of the five non-English-language films.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining counter-type as a representation that challenges an existing stereotype, offering a more complex or alternative portrayal; 1 mark for a relevant example applied to a named film (e.g. Wadjda represents a Saudi girl with agency and desire, countering the stereotype of passive or invisible Muslim girlhood; Girlhood presents Black teenage girls in Paris as subjects of joy and collective self-creation rather than as objects of social concern).

practice_questions.text: Explain how Dennis Gansel uses cinematography and editing in the classroom 'unity' sequence of The Wave to represent conformity as seductive. Refer to specific micro choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific micro choice (e.g. tightening frame from medium shot to medium close-up; warming colour palette; accelerating edit rhythm); 1 mark for a second distinct choice; 1 mark for explaining the effect of the first choice on spectator positioning or representation (e.g. the tightening frame draws the spectator closer into the group’s energy, representing conformity as intimate rather than threatening at this stage); 1 mark for explaining the representational consequence (e.g. the film makes the seduction of fascist unity legible to a contemporary audience, which is the film’s macro representational project); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (cinematography, mise-en-scene, diegetic, representation, spectator positioning).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Lulu Wang uses mise-en-scene and sound in the wedding-banquet hall set piece of The Farewell to represent the tension between Chinese and American cultural values. Refer to at least two specific micro choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two specific mise-en-scene or sound choices are identified within the named sequence (e.g. slow static takes that hold the family in interior warm light without cutting away; the absence of non-diegetic score, replacing it with the ambient sound of the banquet — diegetic chatter, clinking glasses, the sounds of a collective occasion; costume choices that visually separate Billi from older family members). Each choice is linked to a specific representational effect (e.g. the static take forces the spectator to read the family’s body language rather than being moved through the scene by editing, representing family dynamics as something to be observed rather than experienced as plot momentum). Macro representation clearly stated (diasporic identity as a space of cultural tension between truth-telling and protective silence). Specialist vocabulary precise.

Secure: Two choices identified with generally accurate representational effect; named sequence referenced; macro meaning present; mostly accurate vocabulary.

Developing: One choice identified; representational effect implied but not stated; may drift toward plot description; limited vocabulary.

Emerging: Generic description of the sequence; no specific micro choices; no representational analysis.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how one of the five non-English-language films uses specific filmic choices to challenge a stereotype and offer a counter-type representation of a social group. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained thesis argues a specific claim about counter-type representation (e.g. Girlhood represents Black femininity in Paris as a space of collective self-creation rather than social threat, constructed through framing and music choices that make the four friends the source of visual pleasure). At least two named sequences are analysed with concrete micro-features (e.g. hotel-room karaoke set piece: the blue-lit frame that belongs entirely to the four friends, the frontal framing that makes them the spectator’s visual focus rather than objects of surveillance; the opening American-football-game tracking shot: the camera follows the girls rather than the game, immediately establishing their perspective). Gaze theory is applied to a specific shot (e.g. in the hotel-room sequence, the girls look at themselves and each other — the gaze is internal to the group, not directed outward by an external observer). Macro meaning sustained throughout (representation as political project; national cinema and cultural ethics). Specialist vocabulary precise. Evaluative judgement justified.

Secure: Thesis present; two sequences referenced; micro-features identified but analysis may be partial; gaze theory or stereotype/counter-type applied; judgement reached.

Developing: Some relevant points; limited named sequences; analysis may become thematic description rather than filmic analysis; limited vocabulary; weak judgement.

Emerging: Plot summary dominates; no thesis; no named sequences used analytically; representation discussed as theme not construction.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Gavin Hood uses music in the township-arrival opening of Tsotsi to represent post-apartheid South African identity. Refer to the specific role of kwaito music in the sequence.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying the kwaito music as both diegetic street sound and non-diegetic score; 1 mark for explaining the cultural significance of kwaito (a South African urban genre associated with post-apartheid township identity); 1 mark for explaining the effect of its use in this sequence (e.g. positions Tsotsi within a specifically South African cultural landscape; the music signals that this is not a generic African township but a post-apartheid Johannesburg community with its own identity); 1 mark for linking to the representation of the township as ordinary urban space rather than exotic or pitiable (the low-key natural light and the dignified framing work alongside the music); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (diegetic, non-diegetic, representation, mise-en-scene, national cinema).

practice_questions.text: Name the editor of Whiplash (2014) who won the Academy Award for Film Editing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Tom Cross.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'diegetic sound' in film analysis?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that diegetic sound originates from within the world of the story; 1 mark for clarifying that it is audible to the characters as well as the audience (e.g. music a band is performing, dialogue, ambient room sounds).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the shift between handheld camera and locked-off camera in the chair-throwing teaching scene of Whiplash creates two distinct registers of experience for the spectator.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the handheld camera in dialogue passages and the locked-off camera in drumming passages; 1 mark for describing the physical effect of each (handheld = instability, volatility; locked-off = control, precision); 1 mark for explaining the contrast in effect on the spectator (emotional turbulence versus rhythmic order); 1 mark for connecting this to the film's thematic concern (the border between emotional experience and musical discipline); 1 mark for a developed point about how this structural principle reinforces the film's argument about the nature of performance.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how cinematography and sound design in the opening solo-drumming entry sequence of Whiplash establish the film's central power dynamic. Refer to at least three distinct micro-features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Stays inside the named sequence; analyses at least three distinct micro-features (e.g. high-contrast lighting from stage-left, the zoom/reframe movement towards Andrew, the cut to Fletcher's still wide shot, the absence of non-diegetic score); for each feature clearly states what meaning it creates (isolation, increasing pressure, the juxtaposition of movement and stillness as a power dynamic); uses specialist vocabulary throughout (cinematography, extreme close-up, juxtaposition, diegetic, lighting state); effects on the spectator stated not implied.

Secure: Identifies at least two micro-features with generally accurate analysis; connects at least one feature to the theme of power; vocabulary mostly accurate; may not fully unpack each choice.

Developing: Describes what is visible (dark room, close-up shots, Andrew drumming) without fully explaining what these choices create; vocabulary limited; effect on spectator implied.

Emerging: General description of the scene; no specific micro-features identified; descriptive plot recall rather than analysis.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how sound design in the chair-throwing teaching scene of Whiplash positions the spectator in relation to Andrew Neiman's experience of the rehearsal room. Focus specifically on the use of diegetic music as the scene's sole acoustic drive.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses the specific use of diegetic music (the band, Fletcher's counting, drum hits) as the film's only acoustic drive in this sequence with no non-diegetic underlayer; explains why the absence of a separate score matters (the drama is produced entirely from what the characters are doing, which fuses musical performance and emotional ordeal for the spectator); names at least one additional micro-detail (e.g. room acoustics, the sharp strike of a hi-hat marking tempo errors); states the macro effect on spectator positioning (complicity in Andrew's physical and psychological experience); specialist vocabulary precise throughout (diegetic, sound design, acoustic space).

Secure: Identifies diegetic music as the key sound element; explains the effect of having no separate non-diegetic score; connects this to the spectator's experience with mostly accurate vocabulary; may not name additional micro-details.

Developing: Notes that the music is present and important but does not explain the significance of it being diegetic rather than an added score; limited vocabulary; effect on spectator implied not stated.

Emerging: General description of the scene's noise or intensity; no engagement with diegetic/non-diegetic distinction; specialist vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: As a critic of US independent cinema, evaluate how Damien Chazelle uses editing and sound design across two named sequences of Whiplash to position the spectator in relation to Andrew Neiman's ambition. Reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Opens with a clear, arguable thesis about how the film uses editing and sound to make the spectator feel complicit in Andrew's ambition, or about the ambiguity of the film's moral position; analyses at least two named sequences (e.g. chair-throwing teaching scene and closing solo sequence); for each sequence identifies specific micro-features (rhythmic cutting, extreme close-up patterning, diegetic-score technique, handheld/locked-off shift) and links each to a macro effect on spectator positioning; integrates relevant contextual material (Sundance route, $3m budget enabling aesthetic concentration, Tom Cross's editing method); may apply Bordwell's concept of narration as information-withholding to the closing sequence's moral ambiguity; sustains specialist vocabulary; closes with a justified evaluative judgement that takes a position on the ambiguity.

Secure: Has a thesis; covers at least two sequences; uses technical vocabulary with reasonable accuracy; connects at least two micro-features to spectator positioning; judgement present but may not fully account for the film's ambiguity.

Developing: Aware that editing and sound are important but analysis stays descriptive ('the fast cuts make it exciting'); minimal use of specific terminology; evidence drawn from one sequence; no thesis; judgement absent or asserted without support.

Emerging: Retells the plot of Andrew's journey; no thesis; no technical analysis; no named sequences; specialist vocabulary absent or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: Name the term for a recurring musical theme associated with a specific character or idea throughout a film.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: leitmotif (also accept: music motif / recurring motif / character theme).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by a 'sound bridge'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a sound bridge connects two scenes across an edit; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: sound from the next scene begins before the image changes, or sound from the current scene continues into the next image (either direction accepted). Full credit requires both identifying the connection and explaining the timing/mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Choose a specific scene from a film you have studied and explain how one diegetic sound choice contributes to the mood of that sequence. Identify the scene by name.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming the scene; 1 mark for identifying the specific diegetic sound (e.g. ambient noise, dialogue mix, a sound effect); 1 mark for explaining what the sound establishes about the environment or character; 1 mark for stating the effect on the spectator at that moment; 1 mark for using accurate specialist vocabulary (e.g. diegetic, ambient sound, synchronous, Foley).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how non-diegetic sound is used in a named sequence from a film you have studied to position the spectator. Refer to at least two specific sound choices within that sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer identifies at least two distinct non-diegetic sound choices within one named sequence; each choice is linked to a specific, stated effect on the spectator; the analysis moves from micro choice (e.g. a rising string motif, an abrupt cut to silence, the use of a recurring leitmotif) to macro meaning (e.g. signals danger, positions the spectator to share the protagonist's vulnerability, signals narrative consequence); specialist vocabulary is used precisely throughout; the response reads as analysis of how sound creates meaning, not description of what happens.
Secure: At least two sound choices identified and linked to spectator effect; the named sequence is clear; some specialist vocabulary used; the link between micro choice and macro effect is present but may be underdeveloped in places.
Developing: One or two sound choices identified but the analysis is generic ('the music is tense'); specialist vocabulary is thin; effect on spectator is implied rather than stated; may be more descriptive than analytical.
Emerging: Basic identification of a sound element with little or no explanation of effect; no named sequence; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how sound design in one short sequence from a film you have studied combines diegetic and non-diegetic elements to create a specific response in the spectator. Focus on at least three distinct sound features within that sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer stays tightly within one short named sequence; at least three distinct sound features are identified (e.g. ambient diegetic sound, a non-diegetic score entry, a moment of silence or a sound bridge); each feature is linked to a specific effect on the spectator; the distinction between diegetic and non-diegetic is applied correctly throughout; the analysis articulates how the combination of sound elements works as a designed whole; specialist vocabulary is precise and varied (leitmotif, synchronous, ambient, Foley, sound bridge, etc.).
Secure: Three sound features identified within one named sequence; diegetic/non-diegetic distinction correctly applied to most features; effect on spectator present for at least two features; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: One or two sound features identified; may blur diegetic and non-diegetic; effect on spectator implied or limited; sequence not clearly named or not consistently maintained throughout.
Emerging: Identifies a sound element but fails to explain its effect; no clear sequence; descriptive rather than analytical; diegetic/non-diegetic distinction not applied.

practice_questions.text: A director chooses to use silence on the soundtrack at the climax of a sequence rather than scoring it with music. Analyse the effect of this choice on the spectator and explain how it contributes to the meaning of that moment. In your answer, name the film and the sequence you are discussing.
practice_questions.marks:
