At least three distinct micro-features are identified with specific technical and spatial description (e.g. two-shot framing with Wikus larger in the near foreground; layered diegetic sound from three simultaneous sources; intercutting between Wikus's camcorder and the MNU external camera). Each feature is linked precisely to its effect on the spectator or to the macro meaning about bureaucratic power and segregation. The micro-macro connection is explicit at every stage.

Secure: Two or more micro-features identified with reasonable technical description. Effect on spectator or macro meaning stated. May lack the spatial precision or full micro-macro chain expected at Mastering.

Developing: Relevant observations but general ('the camera shakes', 'the sound is busy'). Effect implied rather than stated. May drift slightly into plot description.

Emerging: Basic identification of one technique with little or no analysis of effect. Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the narrative structure of District 9 uses the mockumentary form and the transformation narrative together to position the spectator in relation to the film's political allegory. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear thesis at the opening claims what the structural combination of mockumentary frame and transformation narrative achieves politically and for the spectator. At least two named sequences are analysed (e.g. the opening mockumentary interview sequence and the MNU laboratory transformation sequence). Each is anchored to specific micro-features (shallow depth of field in interviews, locked-off versus handheld grammar, rack focus at eye level during the transformation). Micro choices are linked to macro political meaning at every stage. Specialist vocabulary is used precisely. The essay ends with a justified evaluative judgement on how effectively the formal strategies serve the allegory.

Secure: A thesis is present and maintained. Two named sequences referenced. Micro-macro link made in most paragraphs. Specialist vocabulary mostly accurate. Conclusion present.

Developing: Some structural analysis but plot summary intrudes. Macro political meaning identified but not demonstrated through specific micro evidence. One sequence at most.

Emerging: Plot summary without structural or political analysis. No thesis. Specialist vocabulary thin or absent.

practice_questions.text: How does the two-shot framing in the eviction-notice sequence communicate a power hierarchy between Wikus and the alien residents? Explain the effect on the spectator.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the two-shot as the relevant device; 1 mark for describing the spatial arrangement (Wikus larger in the near foreground, alien smaller further back); 1 mark for explaining how the blocked geography communicates power without dialogue; 1 mark for linking to the spectator's position (placed behind Wikus, sharing his perspective before identification shifts); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (two-shot, blocking, foreground, restricted narration, power).

practice_questions.text: Name the director of The Babadook.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Jennifer Kent.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'narrative catalyst'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a narrative catalyst is an object, person or event that initiates or accelerates the plot; 1 mark for an explanation that the catalyst disrupts the existing equilibrium and sets the story in motion (e.g. the Mister Babadook storybook in the film).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the film's desaturated colour palette contributes to the narrative theme of grief in The Babadook. Refer to one named sequence.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the desaturated palette as the device (cool blues, greys, low contrast); 1 mark for naming a specific sequence (e.g. the children's-book opening reveal sequence, the bedroom doorway confrontation); 1 mark for explaining the palette's connection to Amelia's psychological state; 1 mark for linking to the spectator's experience (palette tells the spectator the home is emotionally cold before the horror begins); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (desaturated palette, mise-en-scene, psychological horror narrative).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Jennifer Kent uses cinematography and blocking in the bedroom doorway confrontation sequence of The Babadook to stage the emotional distance between Amelia and Samuel. Refer to at least three distinct micro-features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays inside the bedroom doorway confrontation sequence throughout. At least three micro-features are identified with specific technical and spatial description (e.g. locked-off two-shot framed through the doorframe; warm bedside lamp on Amelia's side versus bare bulb on Samuel's; the strip of darkness between them; blocking on the threshold). Each is linked precisely to the macro meaning about grief's effect on the mother-son relationship. The spectator's experience is articulated explicitly.

Secure: Two or more micro-features identified with reasonable description. Macro meaning about grief stated. May lack the spatial precision expected at Mastering.

Developing: Relevant but general ('the lighting is dark', 'they are standing at the door'). Effect implied not stated. May drift into plot description.

Emerging: One feature identified with little analysis. Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how Jennifer Kent uses the film's narrative structure to argue that grief cannot be destroyed, only accepted. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement about the effectiveness of the film's final resolution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear thesis argues that the film's narrative structure refuses classical horror resolution in favour of a grief-acceptance arc. At least two named sequences are analysed (e.g. the children's-book opening reveal sequence and the closing basement-feeding ritual). Each is anchored to specific micro-features (slow camera tilt, shallow focus on the pop-up figure, held long take on Amelia descending). Micro choices are linked to macro psychological meaning at every stage. Todorov's model is applied to a named moment — not described in the abstract. Specialist vocabulary precise. The essay ends with a justified evaluative judgement on the effectiveness of the resolution.

Secure: Thesis present. Two sequences referenced. Micro-macro link made in most paragraphs. Theory named and applied. Conclusion present.

Developing: Some argument about grief but plot summary intrudes. One sequence at most. Theory mentioned without application to a moment.

Emerging: Plot summary. No thesis. No named sequences. Specialist vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: How does the sound design in The Babadook use restraint and silence as horror devices? Explain the effect on the spectator with reference to one named sequence.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying restrained or absent sound as the device; 1 mark for naming a specific sequence (e.g. the police-station sequence where ambient domestic sound drops completely); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (contrast between loud domestic diegetic sound and abrupt silence); 1 mark for linking to the spectator's experience (silence more unsettling than a jump scare); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (diegetic sound, non-diegetic score, sound design, psychological horror).

practice_questions.text: Name the director of The Breadwinner.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Nora Twomey.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'frame-tale structure'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a frame-tale structure embeds one story inside another; 1 mark for explaining that one narrative level acts as the container or frame for the inner narrative (e.g. the realist Kabul narrative frames the storybook insets in The Breadwinner).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the shift in colour palette between the realist Kabul sequences and the storybook insets communicates meaning to the spectator in The Breadwinner. Refer to one named sequence.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the two palettes (earth tones for Kabul; jewel tones for the storybook); 1 mark for naming a specific sequence (e.g. the opening market-stall storybook sequence); 1 mark for explaining the chromatic shift as a diegetic-level signal; 1 mark for linking to the spectator's experience (palette shift tells the spectator they have moved from survival to imagination); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (diegetic levels, frame-tale structure, palette, mise-en-scene).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Nora Twomey uses animation style, sound design and figure-to-space ratio in the disguise-haircut transformation scene of The Breadwinner to communicate the significance of the moment. Refer to at least three distinct micro-features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays inside the disguise-haircut transformation scene throughout. At least three distinct micro-features are identified with specific technical and spatial description (e.g. static medium close-up on Parvana's face; simplified flat animation style stripping expression to essential lines; diegetic scissors sound only with non-diegetic score withheld; shadow-striped wall as background). Each is linked precisely to the macro meaning about the weight of the transformation and its significance to Parvana's survival. The spectator's experience is articulated explicitly.

Secure: Two or more micro-features identified with reasonable description. Macro meaning stated. May lack spatial precision expected at Mastering.

Developing: Relevant observations but general. Effect implied not stated. May drift into plot summary.

Emerging: One feature identified with little analysis. Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the frame-tale structure of The Breadwinner uses two narrative levels to argue that storytelling is a form of survival under occupation. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear thesis argues that the film's frame-tale structure deploys the storybook level not as decoration but as a structural parallel that carries the central argument about imagination and survival. At least two named sequences are analysed (e.g. the opening market-stall storybook sequence and the storybook frame-tale insets or the closing reunion sequence). Each is anchored to specific micro-features (chromatic shift, animation-style contrast, figure-to-space ratio, score withholding). Micro choices are linked to macro meaning at every stage. Specialist vocabulary is precise throughout. The essay ends with a justified evaluative judgement.

Secure: Thesis present. Two sequences referenced. Micro-macro link in most paragraphs. Vocabulary mostly accurate. Conclusion present.

Developing: Argument about storytelling and survival present but plot summary intrudes. One sequence at most.

Emerging: Plot summary. No thesis. No sequences. Specialist vocabulary absent.

practice_questions.text: How does the Pul-e-Charkhi prison-visit sequence use figure-to-space ratio to communicate the institution's power over Parvana? Explain the effect on the spectator.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying figure-to-space ratio as the device; 1 mark for describing the composition (prison walls occupy four-fifths of the frame; Parvana is a small figure at the base); 1 mark for explaining the effect of the ratio (institution is visually dominant, individual is diminished); 1 mark for linking to the spectator's shared experience of the prison as immovable and impersonal; 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (figure-to-space ratio, composition, framing, diegetic levels).

practice_questions.text: Name the novel that Jojo Rabbit adapts and its author.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Caging Skies by Christine Leunens. (Accept either the title alone or title plus author.)

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'dramatic irony' in film studies?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that dramatic irony involves a gap in understanding between the spectator and a character; 1 mark for explaining that the spectator knows something the character does not, generating irony, tension or pathos (e.g. the spectator understands the absurdity of Jojo's beliefs while Jojo does not).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the anachronistic music in Jojo Rabbit positions the spectator in a satirical register. Refer to one named sequence.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying anachronistic music as the device; 1 mark for naming a specific sequence (e.g. the imaginary-Hitler dance opening sequence); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (contemporary music placed in a 1940s setting signals a satirical rather than realist register); 1 mark for linking to the spectator's experience (signals that the film will treat fascism as something that can be seen through); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (diegetic, non-diegetic, comic distance, anachronism, satirical register).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Mihai Malaimare Jr. uses cinematography and blocking in the imaginary-Hitler dance opening sequence of Jojo Rabbit to establish the film's child-perspective narrative and comic-distance strategy. Refer to at least three distinct micro-features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays inside the opening sequence throughout. At least three distinct micro-features are identified with specific technical and spatial description (e.g. child's-eye low-angle framing making Adolf slightly over-large; mathematically centred symmetrical two-shot compositions; warm amber-and-red palette; anachronistic non-diegetic music; shot-reverse-shot cutting rhythm applied to real and imaginary character equally). Each is linked precisely to the effect on the spectator (satirical register, warm aesthetic that the spectator must consciously resist, dramatic irony). The micro-macro connection is explicit.

Secure: Two or more micro-features identified with reasonable description. Comic-distance strategy and dramatic irony articulated. May lack spatial precision expected at Mastering.

Developing: Relevant observations but general ('the colours are bright', 'the camera is low'). Effect implied not stated.

Emerging: One feature identified with little analysis. Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: To what extent does Taika Waititi's comic-distance strategy in Jojo Rabbit serve its anti-hate argument? Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear thesis makes a claim about whether and how the comic-distance strategy serves or risks undermining the film's anti-hate thesis. At least two named sequences are analysed (e.g. the imaginary-Hitler dance opening sequence and the public-square hanging sequence). Each is anchored to specific micro-features (symmetrical compositions, low-angle framing, tonal cut, palette continuity between comic and horrific). Micro choices are linked to macro meaning about indoctrination, banality and moral awakening. The evaluative judgement is the essay's destination, not its starting point, and is argued through rather than asserted. Specialist vocabulary precise throughout.

Secure: Thesis present and maintained. Two sequences referenced. Micro-macro link in most paragraphs. Evaluative judgement present. Vocabulary mostly accurate.

Developing: Argument about comic distance present but plot summary intrudes. One sequence at most. Evaluative judgement may be asserted rather than argued.

Emerging: Plot summary. No thesis. No sequences. Vocabulary absent or misapplied.

practice_questions.text: How does the absence of the imaginary Hitler in the attic-discovery moment function as a narrative device to signal the beginning of Jojo's moral awakening? Explain the effect on the spectator.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the absence of the imaginary companion as the device; 1 mark for explaining the formal logic (the imaginary Hitler has been present in every prior scene; his absence in the attic signals a boundary the ideology cannot cross); 1 mark for linking to the moral-awakening arc (Jojo's imagination begins to evict the indoctrinated self as real human encounter takes hold); 1 mark for linking to the spectator's experience (the absence registers immediately because his presence has been so consistent); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (imaginary companion, moral-awakening arc, dramatic irony, child-perspective narration).

practice_questions.text: Identify the cinematographer who shot Tsotsi (2005).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Lance Gewer.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'mise-en-scène' as it is used in film analysis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that mise-en-scène refers to everything placed within or arranged in the frame; 1 mark for listing at least two correct examples of mise-en-scène elements (e.g. set design, costume, lighting, props, blocking, performance).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of handheld camera in the township-arrival opening sequence of Tsotsi positions the spectator in relation to the protagonist and the Soweto setting. What effect does this micro choice produce?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the technique (handheld camera); 1 mark for linking it to the township-arrival opening sequence specifically; 1 mark for explaining the naturalist or unsteady quality the technique creates; 1 mark for explaining the effect on the spectator (e.g. places the spectator inside the volatile space, codes the setting as lived-in rather than exotic); 1 mark for using accurate specialist vocabulary (e.g. naturalism, hand-held, point of view, documentary register).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the childhood-flashback sequence under the concrete pipes uses cinematography and sound design to represent the protagonist's inner life. Refer to at least two distinct micro features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays inside the childhood-flashback sequence and unpacks at least three distinct micro features (e.g. low-angle child-perspective shots, the shift from naturalist to warm overexposed lighting, distorted sound design of raised voices, the cut to the adult face in the present). Every micro feature is linked to a representational meaning — the sequence constructs the protagonist as a trauma survivor, positioning the spectator to understand rather than judge his gang identity. Specialist vocabulary is used precisely throughout. Emerging: Basic identification of one or two features with little explanation of representational effect; the answer drifts toward plot description rather than analysis of how meaning is created.
Secure: At least two micro features identified with explanation of effect on spectator and representational meaning, though one feature may be less precisely anchored to the sequence.
Developing: Relevant features mentioned but generic description dominates; effect on spectator implied rather than stated; specialist vocabulary thin.
Emerging: Basic listing; plot retelling; no named sequence; no specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Tsotsi uses cinematography and mise-en-scène to represent post-apartheid masculinity. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear thesis on how the film's representational project positions the spectator in relation to post-apartheid Black South African masculinity. At least two named sequences analysed in depth with concrete micro features (shot type, lighting state, mise-en-scène elements) linked to macro representational arguments. The kwaito score or sound design may be integrated as further evidence. Reference to the broader post-apartheid context anchors the argument contextually. A justified evaluative judgement on the effectiveness or complexity of the representation closes the essay. Specialist vocabulary used precisely and consistently.
Secure: At least two named sequences referenced with generally concrete micro features; representational argument is present though may lack full development; evaluative judgement is present but may be brief.
Developing: Relevant points but thin micro analysis; representation discussed in vague terms; evaluative judgement may be absent.
Emerging: Largely plot retelling; no clear thesis; no named sequences; little or no specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Compare how cinematography is used in the township-arrival opening and the Miriam apartment-feeding sequence of Tsotsi to represent different aspects of the protagonist's social world. Identify one key difference in the cinematographic approach between the two sequences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An explicit comparative line runs through every paragraph — matching the specific cinematographic choice in each sequence (e.g. hand-held naturalism on the platform versus locked-off static framing in the apartment; low-key exterior lighting versus the brighter, softer key light of the interior), explaining what each choice constructs representationally, and accounting for the contextual difference (the township as volatile public space; the apartment as a possible alternative social world). The response ends with a synthesised judgement about what the contrast between these two representational registers says about post-apartheid South African social geography. Specialist vocabulary is precise.
Secure: Both sequences referenced with at least one specific micro choice per sequence; comparative link is present but may not run through every paragraph; contextual judgement is attempted.
Developing: Both sequences mentioned but treated separately without an explicit comparative line; micro features are vague.
Emerging: Only one sequence discussed or no micro analysis; no comparative structure.

practice_questions.text: Identify the director of The Wave (2008).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Dennis Gansel.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'mise-en-scène' with specific reference to one element used in The Wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct general definition of mise-en-scène (everything placed within the frame to create meaning); 1 mark for correctly identifying and naming one specific element from The Wave (e.g. the white-shirt costume design, the symmetrical classroom framing, the institutional flat lighting).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of costume in the white-shirt uniform-adoption sequence of The Wave represents the concept of conformity. What effect does this micro choice have on the spectator?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the costume change (to matching white shirts) in the white-shirt adoption sequence; 1 mark for linking this to the concept of conformity and the collapsing of individual identity; 1 mark for noting the visual effect on the wide shot (the students become a single visual unit); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the spectator (a simultaneous sense of attraction and unease at the order created); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (e.g. mise-en-scène, wide shot, representation, conformity, uniform).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how cinematography and editing work together in the school playground wave-chant sequence of The Wave to represent the dynamics of group conformity. Stay inside this one sequence and identify at least three distinct micro features.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays inside the playground wave-chant sequence and unpacks at least three distinct micro features (e.g. the shift from locked-off to handheld camera, the increase in edit pace matching the chant rhythm, the non-diegetic score layered over diegetic chanting). Each micro feature is linked to a representational meaning about group belonging and the kinetic pull of conformity. Specialist vocabulary used precisely throughout.
Secure: At least two micro features identified with explanation of effect on spectator; representational argument present though one feature may be less fully developed.
Developing: Relevant features mentioned but spread too thinly across the whole film rather than anchored in the sequence; effect on spectator implied not stated.
Emerging: Basic description of what happens; no named sequence; no specialist vocabulary; no representational argument.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how The Wave represents the relationship between youth identity and conformity. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach an evaluative judgement about how successfully the film constructs this representation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained thesis on how the film represents conformity as initially attractive and only gradually threatening. At least two named sequences analysed with concrete micro features (e.g. locked-off framing in the opening lesson, handheld camera in the playground chant, the return to symmetrical framing in the closing assembly). Micro choices are linked to macro representational arguments about youth, individuality and the conditions that enable fascism. AO1 context (the Ron Jones experiment, the German setting) is integrated to support AO2 analysis rather than to replace it. A justified evaluative judgement closes the essay. Specialist vocabulary precise and consistent.
Secure: At least two named sequences with generally concrete micro features; representational argument present; evaluative judgement attempted.
Developing: Relevant points but thin micro analysis; plot description dominates some paragraphs.
Emerging: Largely retells the plot; no clear thesis; minimal specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast how the opening lesson sequence and the closing assembly-hall sequence of The Wave use cinematography and mise-en-scène to represent the students differently. Match one specific micro choice from each sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An explicit comparative line runs through the response — matching a specific micro choice from each sequence (e.g. flat-lit locked-off framing in the opening vs the same symmetrical frame now filled with identical white shirts in the assembly; varied sartorial mise-en-scène in the opening vs the visual uniformity of the white shirts), explaining what each choice constructs representationally, and accounting for the contextual change across the film. The response ends with a synthesised judgement about what the formal return to locked-off symmetry means for the film's representational argument. Specialist vocabulary precise.
Secure: Both sequences referenced with at least one specific micro choice per sequence; comparative link present but may not run through every paragraph; contextual judgement attempted.
Developing: Both sequences mentioned but treated separately; micro features are vague.
Emerging: Only one sequence discussed; no comparative structure; no representational argument.

practice_questions.text: Identify the director of Wadjda (2012).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Haifaa Al-Mansour.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'representation' as it applies to a global non-English-language film question.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining representation as the way people, groups, places or ideas are constructed and presented to the spectator; 1 mark for specifying that this is achieved through filmic choices (cinematography, mise-en-scène, editing, sound) rather than through plot events.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of doorway and window framing in Wadjda represents the conditions of female life in the film's world. Refer to at least one specific example of this technique and explain its effect on the spectator.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the doorway or window framing technique; 1 mark for naming a specific sequence in which it appears (e.g. the mother observed through the front door, Ms. Hussa framed by the school doorway); 1 mark for explaining what architectural framing does visually (places the figure inside a bounded aperture, limits her visible world); 1 mark for explaining the representational effect on the spectator (the architecture becomes a visual metaphor for social enclosure; restriction appears structural rather than individual); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (e.g. door-frame shot, mise-en-scène, representation, containment, aperture composition).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how cinematography in the toy-shop bicycle reveal and the closing street-traversal sequence of Wadjda constructs the bicycle as a symbol of agency. Refer to specific camera and framing choices in both sequences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response stays within the two named sequences and unpacks distinct micro features in each (e.g. low-angle shot with the glass boundary in the bicycle reveal; the tracking shot matching the camera's movement to the bicycle's freedom in the closing sequence). Each micro feature is linked to a representational argument about girlhood, agency and the right to public space. The comparison between the blocked desire in the reveal and the achieved (if provisional) freedom in the closing tracking shot forms a coherent representational arc. Specialist vocabulary precise throughout.
Secure: Both sequences referenced with at least one concrete micro feature each; representational argument present though one sequence may be less fully developed.
Developing: Both sequences mentioned but analysis is generic; effect on spectator implied not stated.
Emerging: Plot description; no named sequences; minimal specialist vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Haifaa Al-Mansour uses cinematography and mise-en-scène in Wadjda to represent girlhood under restriction. Refer to at least two named sequences and reach an evaluative judgement about how effectively the film constructs this representation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained thesis on how the film represents girlhood under structural rather than individual restriction, making the case that specific filmic choices (low-angle child-eye framing, door-frame and window compositions, the glass-and-bicycle juxtaposition in the bicycle reveal, the tracking shot in the closing sequence) collectively build this argument. At least two named sequences analysed in depth with concrete micro features linked to macro representational meanings. AO1 production context (first Saudi feature, first Saudi female director, Al-Mansour directing from inside a van) is integrated as evidence of the film's representational significance rather than merely recited. A justified evaluative judgement on the complexity or limitations of the representation closes the essay. Specialist vocabulary precise and consistent.
Secure: At least two named sequences with generally concrete micro analysis; representational argument present; evaluative judgement attempted.
